subject: English
description: Voice conversion across tenses, imperatives, and modal constructions

questions.stem: Change to passive voice: 'She wrote a letter.'

options.option_text: A letter is written by her.
A letter was written by her.
A letter has been written by her.
A letter was being written by her.

questions.explanation: Simple past active → past 'to be' + past participle (was/were + V3). 'wrote' → 'was written'. Subject becomes 'by her'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert to passive: 'The teacher is explaining the lesson.'

options.option_text: The lesson is explained by the teacher.
The lesson is being explained by the teacher.
The lesson was being explained by the teacher.
The lesson has been explained by the teacher.

questions.explanation: Present continuous active → is/are + being + V3. 'is explaining' → 'is being explained'.
questions.subject: English

options.option_text: The door is closed.
Let the door be closed.
The door should be closed.
You are closing the door.

questions.explanation: Imperative active → 'Let' + object + 'be' + V3. 'Close the door' → 'Let the door be closed'. The 'should be' form is also acceptable in some textbooks but 'Let ... be' is the canonical conversion for direct imperatives.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Passive form of 'They have completed the project.' is:

options.option_text: The project is completed by them.
The project has been completed by them.
The project had been completed by them.
The project was completed by them.

questions.explanation: Present perfect active → has/have been + V3. 'have completed' → 'has been completed' (subject 'project' is singular, so 'has').
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive: 'Who wrote this novel?'

options.option_text: Who was this novel written by?
By whom this novel was written?
This novel was written by whom?
Whom did write this novel?

questions.explanation: Interrogative 'Who + V_past + object' → 'By whom + was/were + object + V3?' or colloquially 'Who was X V3 by?'. Option A captures the colloquial form. Formally: 'By whom was this novel written?' — which is not offered here.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Passive of 'You must follow the instructions.' is:

options.option_text: Instructions must be followed.
The instructions are followed by you.
You are followed by instructions.
The instructions had been followed.

questions.explanation: Modal (must/should/can/may) + V_base → modal + be + V3. 'You must follow X' → 'X must be followed [by you]'. 'By you' is often dropped because the agent is generic.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the sentence already in the PASSIVE voice:

options.option_text: The children are playing in the garden.
He had forgotten his umbrella.
The bridge was built in 1965.
She will call you tomorrow.

questions.explanation: 'The bridge was built' = subject receives the action → passive. The others are active (subject performs the action).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which option correctly converts 'They will launch the new satellite next month' into passive voice?

options.option_text: The new satellite will be launching next month.
The new satellite will be launched next month.
The new satellite would be launched next month.
The new satellite is being launched next month.

questions.explanation: B is correct: simple future passive = will + be + past participle (will be launched). Option A uses a progressive form 'will be launching' which is not a valid passive structure. Option C introduces 'would', shifting the meaning to conditional. Option D uses present continuous passive, mismatching the future time frame.

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive voice form of 'The committee selects candidates through written interviews'?

options.option_text: Candidates are being selected by the committee through written interviews.
Candidates were selected by the committee through written interviews.
Candidates are selected by the committee through written interviews.
Candidates have been selected by the committee through written interviews.

questions.explanation: C is correct: simple present active (selects) → simple present passive (are selected). Option A (are being selected) is the passive of 'is currently selecting' — present continuous. Option B (were selected) shifts to simple past. Option D (have been selected) is present perfect passive, implying completion rather than habitual action.

questions.stem: Identify the correct passive transformation of 'The chef was preparing a special dish for the guests when the owner arrived'?

options.option_text: A special dish was being prepared for the guests by the chef when the owner arrived.
A special dish was prepared for the guests by the chef when the owner arrived.
A special dish had been prepared for the guests by the chef when the owner arrived.
A special dish is being prepared for the guests by the chef when the owner arrived.

questions.explanation: A is correct: past continuous active (was preparing) → past continuous passive (was being + V3). Option B (was prepared) is simple past passive — wrong tense. The most common mistake is Option B; candidates forget the 'being' in progressive passives. Option C uses past perfect, and Option D incorrectly uses present continuous despite a clearly past-tense context clue ('when the owner arrived').

questions.stem: When 'The principal awarded Riya the gold medal' is converted into passive voice, which form is grammatically correct?

options.option_text: The gold medal was awarded Riya by the principal.
Riya was awarded the gold medal by the principal.
The gold medal was awarded to Riya from the principal.
Riya has been awarded the gold medal by the principal.

questions.explanation: B is correct: with two objects (indirect object = Riya, direct object = the gold medal), the indirect object preferentially becomes the subject in passive voice: 'Riya was awarded the gold medal by the principal.' Option A drops the required preposition 'to' if the direct object is fronted. Option C incorrectly uses 'from' instead of 'by' for the agent. Option D shifts the tense to present perfect without justification.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly renders 'Someone had stolen my bicycle before I reached home' in passive voice?

options.option_text: My bicycle had been stolen before I reached home.
My bicycle was stolen before I reached home by someone.
My bicycle has been stolen before I reached home.
My bicycle had stolen before I reached home by someone.

questions.explanation: A is correct: past perfect active (had + stolen) → past perfect passive (had been + V3 = had been stolen); the indefinite agent 'someone' is dropped as it adds no information. Option B uses simple past passive, losing the past-perfect aspect that signals prior completion. Option C uses present perfect, changing the tense entirely. Option D omits 'been', producing a non-passive, ungrammatical structure.

questions.stem: Three of the following passive constructions are grammatically correct. Which one contains an error?

options.option_text: The letter was being written by him when I called.
The homework must have been completed by the students by noon.
The awards have been distributed to all eligible winners.
The new bridge is been built by the state engineers.

questions.explanation: D is the erroneous sentence: 'is been built' is not a valid English passive form. The present continuous passive requires 'is being built' (is + being + V3). Options A (past continuous passive), B (modal perfect passive: must + have been + V3), and C (present perfect passive) are all correctly formed. Candidates frequently confuse 'is been' with 'is being' under exam pressure.

questions.stem: Which option correctly converts the present continuous active sentence 'The authorities are looking into all complaints filed last week' into passive voice?

options.option_text: All complaints filed last week are looked into by the authorities.
All complaints filed last week are being looked into by the authorities.
All complaints filed last week were being looked into by the authorities.
All complaints filed last week have been looked into by the authorities.

questions.explanation: B is correct: present continuous passive = am/is/are + being + V3; crucially, the phrasal verb 'look into' must remain intact — splitting it into 'looked by ... into' is a known error. Option A (are looked into) is simple present passive, not continuous. Option C (were being) shifts to past continuous. Option D (have been looked into) is present perfect passive. This question tests both tense accuracy and phrasal verb passivisation — a paired challenge that trips many candidates.
